name: what-i-say
title: What I Actually Say
kicker: Dictation, through /remote-control · AI in the loop, in practice
html:
What I Actually Say

Mostly, I talk. Speech-to-text, into a phone, through /remote-control.

I Own the Goal

One sentence, said out loud.

I Don’t Approve Every Step

The hooks hold the order while nobody watches.

I Read the Record Afterward

Which scenario, which red run, which green run, which commit.

/remote-control

Please give me an update

Red run logged: 3 failures, on behavior. Writing the fix.

How’s it going?

Green. Commit gate: TDD order checked.

go deep on bed gates skill

The bdd-gates skill, understood.

Illustrative, not a transcript. The two questions are the real ones. So is “bed gates”.
say: Mostly, I talk. Most evenings it's the same two questions into my phone: 'Please give me an update', and 'How's it going?' Dictation has opinions of its own; it hears 'BDD gates' as 'bed gates' about half the time. Claude knows what I mean, and the gates don't care either way. What I don't do is approve every step. I own the goal, I say it in a sentence, and afterward I read the record: which scenario, which red run, which green run, which commit. People call that AI in the loop: the person in control, the AI in support. So what did months of that produce?

deck:ref.name: no-time
deck:ref.label: NO-TIME
deck:ref.title: No time to type
deck:ref.summary: Family and a new dog took the typing time: one hand on a leash, a phone in the other. Half the fix is Claude Code's /remote-control: the session runs on my machine, steered mostly by speech-to-text dictation. The other half is rigour without watching: the agent must behave the same way every time and follow BDD strictly (Gherkin, red, code, green, commit), so hooks enforce the order and log every run, and the record is read later instead of the agent being monitored. Controls that hold while nobody watches: what this talk asks of agents calling APIs too.

deck:ref.name: ai-in-the-loop
deck:ref.label: AI-IN-THE-LOOP
deck:ref.title: AI in the loop: the person in control, the AI in support
deck:ref.summary: Natarajan, Mathur, Sidheekh, Stammer and Kersting contrast human-in-the-loop systems with AI-in-the-loop (AI²L) systems, where the human is in control of the system and the AI is there to support the human, and argue that evaluations should not judge the machine component alone.
deck:ref.quote: “We argue that existing evaluation methods often overemphasize the machine (learning) component's performance, neglecting the human expert's critical role.”
deck:ref.cite: Natarajan, Mathur, Sidheekh, Stammer and Kersting, “Human-in-the-loop or AI-in-the-loop? Automate or Collaborate?”, arXiv
